In brief

When the Citizen exclaims, "Save the trees of Ireland for the future men of Ireland on the fair hills of Eire, O," his final words quote the frequently repeated refrain of a 17th or 18th century Irish-language poem that James Clarence Mangan translated into English in the 19th century. The poem had long been associated with a traditional Irish melody, so the Citizen may know it as a song.

At more length

Spoken by an exile longing for the natural beauties of his native land, the poem mixes romantic appreciation of the landscape with lamentation for "Eirè's decay" (6). Both themes are relevant to the context in Cyclops. The Citizen, responding to John Wyse Nolan's deforestation concerns, recalls famous great trees of the Irish past and then speaks of saving what is left. No doubt he is recalling lines 13-16 of the poem:

Her woods are tall and straight, grove rising over grove,
Trees flourish in her glens below and on her heights above;
Ah! in heart and in soul I shall ever, ever love
The fair hills of Eirè, O!

The refrain sounds 18 times, making it tedious to read on the page, and the other 30 lines are not especially interesting—repetitious raptures of monochromatic patriotism calculated to appeal to someone like the Citizen. Sung, however, the lines are much more effective. In particular, the musical phrase "Eirè, O" possesses a lilting magic remarkably like the "O" constructions in the Scottish folk ballad Fennario.

John Hunt 2026
